Learning Objectives
Outline common ligamentous knee injury patterns in pediatric athletes.
Assess the evaluation criteria for a pediatric athlete with an acute knee injury.
Identify and compare the risks associated with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in
skeletally immature patients and adult patients.
Describe and compare the principles of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in skeletally
immature patients and adult patients.
Describe and compare the risk of anterior cruciate ligament reinjury after ligament
reconstruction in skeletally immature patients and adult patients.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are increasing in the adolescent population.
Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprains are the most common ligament tears in the pediatric
knee but rarely require surgical management. Complete MCL tears occur less frequently.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) and lateral collateral ligament (LCL) tears are relatively less
frequent in adolescents.
Ligaments fail if loaded at speeds and forces that elongate the ligament to more than 10% of
its original length.
Approximately 70% of ACL tears result from noncontact injuries, and approximately 30% of
ACL tears result from contact injuries.
Approximately 70% of patients with hemarthrosis of the knee after an acute injury also have
an ACL injury.
Epidemiology
Tibial spine fractures were once thought to be the pediatric equivalent of midsubstance ACL
tears.
ACL tears occur more frequently than tibial spine fractures, even in pediatric patients.
The peak incidence for ACL tears is late teens to early twenties.
Females are almost twice as likely to tear their ACL than males while playing the same sport1
(Resource 1).
Annual incidence of ACL injuries has been estimated to be as high as 4% to 5% for females
playing year-round, high-risk sports, such as soccer.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The pediatric knee is stabilized by the same ligamentous structures found in the adult knee.
ACL
PCL
MCL (superficial and deep) and posteromedial corner complex
LCL and posterolateral corner complex
Ligamentous stabilizers are more lax in younger children and tighten toward the end of
growth.

The Lachman test in a pediatric knee may reveal substantially more translation than that in an
adult knee relative to the size of the knee. Physical examination of the contralateral knee often
may reveal the normal state of the knee for a child at that stage of development.
The origin and insertion of the ACL relative to the physis influences reconstruction options in
skeletally immature patients.
Osteology
Most of the longitudinal growth of the lower extremities is from the distal femoral and
proximal tibial physes.
Circumferential growth occurs via the periosteum in the metaphyseal and diaphyseal
segments and through the secondary physis in the subchondral region at the joint surface.
Damage involving more than 7% of the total physeal area increases the risk of growth
disturbance2-4
Rigid fixation or bone blocks across a physis may cause growth disturbance.
Eccentric/peripheral damage to the physis and damage to the perichondral ring are associated
with a greater risk of growth disturbance than injuries to the central portion of the physis.
Tunnels drilled across a physis may result in a decreased risk of growth disturbance if a soft-
tissue graft is placed in the tunnel.
Excessive tensioning of a soft-tissue graft across the physis has been shown to cause growth
disturbance in animal models and, therefore, should be avoided in patients with considerable
growth remaining.
Varus and valgus deformities place excessive stress on the LCL and MCL.
Increased posterior slope of the tibia increases anterior force on the tibia if the knee is loaded
in compression.

Osteology
The anatomic localization of ligament reconstruction procedures that involve docking a
graft into a bony tunnel may change over time as bony structures grow and develop.
This is most evident with medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction that involve
docking a graft into the distal femur just proximal to the physis. With growth, the femoral
attachment may migrate proximally; therefore, the graft biomechanics may be markedly
altered. Epiphyseal ACL tunnels may be appropriately placed at the time of

Nerves
The knee ligaments are innervated and provide substantial proprioceptive feedback about
knee position and function.
Joints and Ligaments
The ACL, MCL, and LCL attach to the femoral epiphysis close to the femoral physis.
The PCL tibial attachment spans the proximal tibial physis.

Joints and Ligaments
The ACL inserts onto the distal femoral epiphysis a few millimeters from the femoral
physis and the posterior periochondrial ring. The tibial insertion is onto the medial tibial
spine. The PCL inserts onto the femoral epiphysis away from the femoral physis;
however, the tibial insertion spans the proximal tibial physis. The MCL inserts onto the
femoral epiphysis a few millimeters from the distal femoral physis, and the tibial
insertion of the superficial MCL is distal to the proximal tibial physis. The LCL inserts
onto the femoral epiphysis a few millimeters from the distal femoral physis, and the
distal insertion is on the proximal tip of the fibular epiphysis.
Musculature
The quadriceps musculature extends the knee but also produces an anteriorly directed force
on the tibia.
The hamstrings flex the knee and produce a posteriorly directed force on the tibia.

Force generated during an eccentric quadriceps muscle contraction that is not balanced
by the hamstrings may result in ACL rupture. Force generated by the hamstrings may
dynamically protect the ACL. The greater the degree of knee flexion, the greater the
posteriorly directed force of the hamstrings.
Knee flexion appears to protect the ACL from injury by placing the hamstrings into a
better position to stress shield the ACL. Knee flexion also decreases the anterior force
generated by an excessive posterior tibial slope.
A hamstring-to-quadriceps strength ratio greater than 0.6 is ideal to ensure that the
quadriceps do not overwhelm hamstring strength and place excess force on the ACL
during activity.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Approximately 70% of all knee ligament injuries occur via a noncontact mechanism of injury.
Approximately 30% of all knee ligament injuries occur via a contact mechanism of injury (eg,
direct blow to the knee/leg).
Risk Factors
Female sex
Females are almost twice as likely as males to sustain an ACL tear while playing the same
sport.
Participation in cutting and pivoting sports activity
High-risk sports include soccer, football, basketball, lacrosse, field hockey, and skiing.
Landing patterns that involve a relatively straight leg and that allow for internal rotation at the
hip or place a valgus force on the knee

Risk Factors
Most noncontact injuries that occur during activities occur in this landing pattern, which
is referred to as dynamic valgus. In the clinical setting, this landing pattern may be

Associated Injuries
Meniscal injuries
The incidence and severity of meniscal tears increase with time if ACL injuries are not
reconstructed.
Cartilage injuries
Damage to the cartilage increases with time if ACL injuries are not reconstructed.
Injury Classification
Ligament injuries are graded according to the severity of injury of each ligament.
Grade 1 (mild/sprain)
Ligament stretched
Pain if stretched on physical examination
Ligament with firm end point and same overall length on physical examination
MRI findings may reveal edema around the structure but no interstitial signal.
Grade 2 (moderate/partial tear)
Ligament partially torn
Pain if stretched on physical examination
Ligament will allow more excursion compared with the uninjured side but may have a firm
end point.
MRI findings reveal discontinuity of some fibers and interstitial signal; however, some fibers
will remain in continuity.
Grade 3 (severe/complete tear)
Ligament completely torn
Pain usually noted on physical examination
Ligament will provide no restraint to manual stress; no firm end point will be felt.
MRI findings do not reveal any fibers in continuity.

Patient History
Mechanism of injury
Contact injury/traumatic injury: direct blow while playing sports, motor vehicle collision, etc.
Noncontact injury: pivoting or shifting injury while playing sports
Timeline of swelling
Effusions that occur immediately postinjury strongly indicate an intra-articular fracture or
capsular disruption.
Effusions that occur a few hours postinjury indicate a slower rate of bleeding and are more
characteristic of an ACL tear and/or a meniscal tear.
A knee effusion does not always occur in patients with an isolated collateral ligament injury.
Extra-articular soft-tissue swelling is more characteristic of these injuries.
Limitations in range of motion (ROM) are common with ligament injuries but also may be
caused by other traumatic knee injuries.
Physical Examination
Consider obtaining radiographs before performing any ligamentous stress tests in a pediatric
patient.
Pediatric patients with substantial acute knee injuries may have physeal fractures that may
displace with standard physical examination maneuvers used to assess the integrity of the
knee ligaments.
Physical examination may be difficult in the acute setting because of pain and/or patient
anxiety.
Areas of point tenderness may help localize the site of the ligament injury.
Ligament injuries usually can be graded clinically.
Intact: firm end point, no pain if stressed
Grade 1: firm end point, pain over the ligament if stressed
Grade 2: some asymmetry in laxity/movement on stress testing, pain over the ligament if
stressed, firm end point on physical examination
Grade 3: markedly increased laxity/movement on stress testing, marked pain if stressed, soft
end point on physical examination

Mechanical block to ROM should prompt evaluation via MRI to determine if meniscal injury is

Neurovascular Examination
Multiligamentous knee injuries are associated with a higher rate of vascular injury; therefore,
patients should be carefully monitored.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs for patients with an acute knee injury should include AP, lateral, and oblique
views to decrease the likelihood of a missed subtle physeal fracture.
Stress radiographs usually are obtained only to evaluate laxity.

Radiography
Despite historical recommendations for stress radiographs to diagnose ligamentous
injuries, MRI has supplanted radiography in the evaluation of pediatric patients because
stress radiographs are associated with a risk for displacing a nondisplaced physeal
fracture.

MRI is useful in confirming a suspected diagnosis or if an adequate physical examination is not

Indicated in most patients with an effusion after an acute knee injury
Expedited imaging studies should be performed in patients with acute loss of motion if clinical
suspicion of a mechanical block exists.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Bucket-handle meniscus tears and displaced chondral fragments are common causes of
acute ROM loss of in a knee joint after an acute injury. Prompt diagnosis and
management of these injuries may markedly affect treatment options, increase the
surgical success rate, and improve long-term outcomes for these patients.

Management
Factors that should be considered
Ligament injured
Skeletal maturity and amount of growth remaining
Injury severity
Concomitant injuries
Meniscal tears
Cartilage injuries
Anticipated future activity level
Functional instability with activities of daily living
All ligament reconstruction procedures in the skeletally immature knee are associated with a
risk of damage to the physis or the perichondrial ring, which may result in a growth
disturbance.
Treatment decisions must balance the risk of iatrogenic physeal injury from a reconstruction
procedure with the risk of ongoing joint damage that may occur in an unreconstructed,
unstable knee.
The consequences of a growth disturbance are greater in patients with more than 1 to 2 years
of growth remaining; therefore, additional caution should be exercised in making treatment
decisions for these patients.
Skeletal age (bone age) and developmental staging techniques (ie, onset of menses) are more
reliable with regard to predicting skeletal maturity and growth remaining than
calendar/chronologic age.

Concomitant meniscal tears and chondral injuries should be repaired if possible.
Complete PCL injuries usually cause less instability than ACL tears but may be associated with
the same risk for long-term arthritis; however, surgical management is more easily avoided
until skeletal maturity.
Nonsurgical Management
Partial tears of the ACL, PCL, MCL, or LCL without other intra-articular pathology (eg, meniscal
tear) are amenable to nonsurgical management.
ACL reconstruction should be considered in patients with a complete ACL tear to avoid
additional meniscal and chondral injury.
Early degenerative changes are present 4 to 5 years postinjury in more than 50% of patients
with a complete ACL tear managed nonsurgically.5
The risk of ongoing injury is increased in patients with greater instability, as measured via KT-
1000 arthrometry, and in patients who elect to continue participation in high-risk sports.6
ACL reconstruction has not been shown to decrease the long-term risk of arthritis.
Complete MCL and PCL injuries often are amenable to nonsurgical management.
Distal MCL injuries with retraction over the pes tendons at the proximal medial tibia (Stener-
like MCL lesions) are associated with decreased healing potential.
Activity modifications, a brief period of immobilization, physical therapy, and pain modalities
are initially indicated for all patients immediately postinjury.

Nonsurgical Management
Patients with a complete ACL tear may experience shifting or buckling instability
episodes in the affected knee postinjury. Patients who experience instability episodes
with activities of daily living should undergo ACL reconstruction via an appropriate
growth-respecting technique irrespective of their age. Some patients with a complete
ACL tear can stabilize the knee via muscular control and never experience any instability
in the knee; these patients are referred to as copers. Many copers can return to activities
without causing additional damage to the knee. Conversely, many other asymptomatic
patients sustain considerable meniscal and articular cartilage damage in the knee. This
damage is difficult to manage surgically and is associated with a high risk for future
arthritis. Different health systems, cultures, physicians, patients, and families weigh

able to adhere to the postoperative rehabilitation regimen. This approach requires more
patients to undergo a surgical procedure with a lengthy rehabilitation; however, it may
provide more patients with a better clinical outcome.

Techniques/Procedures
Some surgeons advocate limiting terminal extension/hyperextension for the first 4 to 6
weeks postinjury to prevent excessive stretch on the healing ACL. Because the ACL
tightens in the last 20° to 30° of knee extension, immobilization with the knee fully
extended may promote ACL healing in an elongated position. Other surgeons have
concerns regarding prolonged periods of limited knee extension because after knee
extension is lost, it often is difficult to restore.
Physical therapy goals include swelling control, pain control, regaining full ROM (after
first 4-week ROM limitations), muscle activation and strengthening, crutch use, and gait
retraining. Physical therapists play a key role in reinforcing activity restrictions.
Many suggest using a battery of strength and functional tests to assess readiness for
return to sports activity. These include a detailed assessment of lower extremity strength
via isokinetic strength testing to ensure that all muscle groups, including the quadriceps
and hamstrings, are within 10% of that of the contralateral limb (90% limb symmetry
index) and that hamstring strength is adequate to balance quadriceps strength. A
hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio higher than 0.6 is ideal to help the hamstrings protect the
ACL. Functional tests to assess coordinated movement patterns during dynamic activities
include balance tests (eg, Y-balance test), a battery of hop tests, (eg, single-leg hop test,
triple hop test, crossover hop tests), and jump landing tests, (eg, drop-landing jump test,

calculation of limb symmetry, and most use 85% to 90% as the cutoff value for return to
sports activity. Subjective movement quality assessments also help predict the risk for
reinjury in deciding the timing of return to sports activity. Neuromuscular training
programs, often referred to as injury prevention programs, are effective at decreasing

Although some data indicate that the use of a functional ACL brace may prevent another
ACL injury in most mainstream sports, this has not been thoroughly studied. Bracing
may promote proper landing mechanics and movement patterns that protect against an
ACL injury, and no studies suggest that bracing increases the risk of repeat injury.

Techniques/Procedures
General principles
No bone plugs should cross the physis (no bone-patellar tendon-bone grafts with bone
blocks across the physis).
No hardware should cross the physis (no interference screws across the physis).
Avoid large tunnels.
Tunnels greater than 5% to 7% of the physeal area are associated with a greater risk of
growth disturbance.
Oblique tunnels create a larger area of physeal damage compared with more
perpendicular tunnels of the same diameter.
Avoid eccentric tunnels.
Avoid damage to the perichondrial ring.
Avoid proximal notchplasty.
Place a soft-tissue graft into the tunnel if a tunnel is drilled across the physis.
Avoid over-tensioning graft across the physis in patients with substantial growth remaining.

Preoperative Planning
A patient who is unable to actively participate in the rehabilitation process or who is
unable or unwilling to maintain appropriate activity restrictions postoperatively may
have poorer outcomes with surgical treatment rather than without surgical treatment.
Heightened anxiety may limit the ability to restore knee motion postoperatively, leading
to arthrofibrosis. Uncontrolled activity in the early postoperative period may lead to
early graft rupture, negating the advantages of early knee stabilization and ultimately
making revision procedures more difficult. Careful shared decision making should be
performed with these patients and their families to determine the best treatment
approach; however, delaying surgical treatment until a patient is able and willing to
safely participate in all aspects of their care often is the best approach.

All-epiphyseal ACL Reconstruction
Graft harvest (quadriceps tendon autograft)
A longitudinal incision is made at the level of the distal quadriceps, and the proximal patella
and quadriceps tendon are exposed.
The paratenon over the distal quadriceps is split and raised distally over the patella and
proximally as far as it can be distinguished as a separate layer.
A central strip of quadriceps tendon approximately 1 cm wide is marked to allow for a graft
approximately 60 mm in length.
The quadriceps tendon is scored (partial thickness) with the use of a double-bladed knife.
The periosteal attachment of the quadriceps onto the patella is elevated.
A near–full-thickness quadriceps tendon graft of approximately 60 mm is harvested, moving
proximally along the fibers of the tendon.
The wound is copiously irrigated.
The rectus tendon is reinforced into the proximal part of the harvest site with the use of
high-strength nonabsorbable suture.
The superficial fibers are loosely reapproximated.
The paratenon is repaired over the harvest site.
A damp sponge is placed in the wound, but the wound not closed at this point.
Graft preparation
The overall graft length usually is approximately 60 mm.
Both ends of the graft are prepared similarly by securing a self-cinching loop fixation device
and a separate set regular, high-strength sutures.
The graft is preconditioned with tension and compression.
Fixation sutures are used to apply approximately 15 to 20 lbs of tension to remove creep in
the graft, which minimizes graft elongation after implantation.
Cylindrical sizing blocks are placed on each end of the graft to gently compress it.
Compression reduces the size of the tunnel necessary to insert the graft, which decreases
the amount of bone removed and improves the safety of the procedure in patients with
small knees.
The graft is resized just before implantation so the smallest-diameter tunnel is used for
implantation.
Knee arthroscopy
Standard anterolateral and anteromedial knee arthroscopy portals are created, and
diagnostic arthroscopy is performed.

The femoral footprint is visualized through the medial portal, and a pediatric-specific femoral

the lateral portal.
An incision is made at the proximal medial tibia lateral to the tibial tubercle, and dissection is
carried down to the level of the periosteum.
A guide pin is then drilled from just above the tibial physis to the center of the tibial physis.
The position of the guide pins is assessed via fluoroscopy.
Standard fluoroscopic imaging techniques may make determination of the anticipated
tunnel location relative to the physis difficult because of the undulations of the distal
femoral and proximal tibial physes; however, experienced surgeons may be able to use this
imaging modality to safely assess tunnel position.
Intraoperative, low-dose, limited CT can be performed to accurately assess pin placement
relative to the physis and predict physeal disruption based on the anticipated final tunnel
size.
Guide pins can be repositioned if necessary.

The iliotibial band at the lateral femur is split around the guide pin.
Drill sleeves are placed over the guide pins and secured into the bone at the outer femoral
and tibial cortices.
Guide pins are removed and replaced with a reverse-cutting drill of the appropriate size
based on the preconditioned size of the graft.
Graft tunnels are then created by back-cutting sockets into the femur and tibia.
Debris is collected with the use of a shaver while drilling the sockets.

Graft fixation
The graft is centered in the knee by applying differential tension on the tibial and femoral
sides of the graft.
The cortical buttons, either pre-attached or attached to the self-cinching loop after suture
passage, are provisionally tightened down against the lateral femoral and proximal tibial
cortices with the knee in full extension.
Graft position and impingement are evaluated through full knee ROM.
Final graft fixation is accomplished on one side of the graft by tying knots in the tails of the
self-cinching loop device and tying the additional whip stitch sutures to the cortical fixation
device.
For all-epiphyseal techniques, the tibial tunnel often is the shortest; therefore, the graft often
is fully seated in the tibial tunnel, leaving the femoral tunnel with a small amount of
additional space to accommodate fully tensioning the graft.
The knee is cycled at least 20 times with the graft under tension and then brought into full
extension.
Tension should be applied to only the non–self-cinching sutures as the knee is cycled to

All-epiphyseal ACL Reconstruction
Multiple techniques have been described for this procedure. The various approaches
involve the use of different strategies based on constantly evolving technology for
creating arthroscopic tunnels and graft fixation techniques; however, all approaches
adhere to the same basic tenets, namely that the graft should enter the knee at the
anatomic footprint of the ACL and that all graft tunnels and fixation should be
contained within the distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphysis.
Postoperative Management
Physical therapy in pediatric patients often is more successful if the physical therapist has
experience working with children and makes rehabilitation interesting and fun.
Compliance with postoperative protocols often is a challenge and should be carefully
monitored.

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Diagnosis
Skeletally immature patients have notably more ligamentous laxity relative to the size of the
knee; therefore, bilateral examination must be performed to assess for asymmetric laxity.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis of ligament injuries in pediatric
patients.
Acute loss of motion after a traumatic knee injury should prompt a timely evaluation via MRI.
Graft
All–soft-tissue grafts are preferred in pediatric patients to avoid hard fixation or bone blocks
crossing the physis.
For socket techniques, the graft length cannot exceed the combined length of both tunnels
plus the intra-articular length of the ACL; therefore, graft lengths usually are shorter in

decrease the diameter of the tunnels/sockets necessary to implant the graft and decrease

Grafts at least 8 mm in diameter are associated with a lower risk of early re-tear.
Tunnels and fixation
Large and oblique tunnels that cross the physis should be avoided in patients with
considerable growth remaining because they increase the likelihood of growth arrest.
No rigid fixation should ever cross the physis.
No bone blocks should ever cross the physis.
Aggressive proximal notchplasty should be avoided to minimize risk to the perichondrial ring
of the physis.
Treatment decision
Consider emotional maturity and ability to maintain postoperative activity restrictions when
making shared treatment decisions with the patient and their family.
Injury prevention
Reinjury rates decrease the longer patients wait to return to sports activity after ACL
reconstruction.
Injury-prevention programs, also known as neuromuscular training programs, may help
decrease the rate of ligament injuries.
Functional bracing during sports activity for as many as 1 to 2 years postoperatively is
advocated by many surgeons; however, little data support this recommendation.
